La Bayadère. A full-length ballet choreographed by Marius Petipa in 1877, set in ancient India and centered on a doomed romance between a warrior and a temple dancer. The work features one of ballet's most famous acts: the Kingdom of the Shades, a visually stunning corps de ballet sequence of identical poses and formations that exemplify the precision and unity of classical ensemble work.

Petipa created the role of Nikiya, the bayadère or sacred temple dancer, as a romantic heroine. Her variations showcase both soft, flowing movement and demanding technical passages. The Kingdom of the Shades sequence in Act III is a parade of identical arabesques followed by a seemingly endless line of corps dancers descending a ramp in synchronized diagonal formations—an icon of classical ballet geometry and discipline.

A fatal snake in a basket scene in Act II provides the drama: a cobra kills Nikiya, setting up the tragic ending and the ghostly encounters of Act III. Minkus' score employs orientalist themes and rhythms, reflecting nineteenth-century European fascination with the exotic East.

The warrior Solor is the male lead, danced with a classical, aristocratic quality. He performs variations that display technical prowess while expressing romantic longing and anguish. The mime sequences, particularly Nikiya's reactions to betrayal and the poison snake, remain a benchmark for classical ballet pantomime.

The ballet is considered a milestone in ballet structure, combining character work, spectacle, pantomime, and pure dance into a unified five-act narrative. The work connects to Petipa, the master choreographer who defined classical ballet form, and to Minkus, the composer who provided the orientalist, romantic score. The ballet draws on Indian culture as its exotic setting and represents a cornerstone classical-era full-length work.
